ann_18.original: identity_age_body = (0.372*age - 0.242*bmi) in standardised units, read into the log-risk with weight one: a plain weighted sum of two inputs. In clinical units, each additional year of age multiplies the hazard by 1.026 (hazard ratio 1.45 per standard deviation of age) and each additional kg/m² of body-mass index multiplies it by 0.957 (0.79 per standard deviation), each through its own edge. The model therefore gives older and thinner patients a higher predicted risk: between the patients at the 5th and the 95th percentile of age the age term changes the hazard 3.19-fold, and the body-mass term 2.29-fold. Self-probe (whole model, the other inputs held at the typical case): sweeping age from 45 to 95 years raises the predicted 3-year risk of death from 17% to 49%; sweeping body-mass index from 20 to 40 kg/m² lowers it from 38% to 18%. On the training split the 156 patients older than 72 have a mean predicted 3-year risk of 53% and 67% of them died during follow-up, against 22% and 20% for the 164 aged 72 or under; this part's mean contribution to the log-risk is 0.41 for the older group and -0.39 for the younger. Switching the part off (its exit fixed at its mean over the training rows) lowers the AUC of the score against the event indicator from 0.833 to 0.781, the largest loss among the four parts (the root lists them). Meaning: age by itself predicts the part's exit with r² 0.82 (meaningful); age and body-mass index are correlated at -0.40 in the training rows, so in the data the two terms partly offset each other. Proportional-hazards caveat: the model can represent a time-constant multiplicative effect of age and body-mass index on the hazard and nothing else; this is not evidence that the effect is constant over follow-up.
ann_18.proposed: Older age raises the hazard steadily; a higher body mass index lowers it steadily.

ann_19.original: identity_haemo = (0.286*hr - 0.199*diasbp - 0.0289*sysbp) in standardised units, read into the log-risk with weight one: a plain weighted sum of the three admission haemodynamic measurements. In clinical units, each additional beat per minute of admission heart rate multiplies the hazard by 1.0121 (1.33 per standard deviation), each additional mm Hg of diastolic blood pressure multiplies it by 0.9908 (0.82 per standard deviation), and each additional mm Hg of systolic blood pressure by 0.9991 (0.972 per standard deviation), each through its own edge. The systolic term is small: between the patients at the 5th and the 95th percentile it changes the hazard 1.10-fold, against 2.44-fold for heart rate and 1.82-fold for diastolic pressure. The model therefore gives a faster heart rate and a lower diastolic pressure at admission a higher predicted risk, a reading of haemodynamic strain. Self-probe (whole model, the other inputs held at the typical case): sweeping heart rate from 50 to 150 beats per minute raises the predicted 3-year risk of death from 22% to 56%; sweeping diastolic pressure from 50 to 120 mm Hg lowers it from 38% to 22%; sweeping systolic pressure from 90 to 200 mm Hg moves it from 32% to 30%. On the training split the 154 patients with an admission heart rate above 85 have a mean predicted 3-year risk of 49% and 59% of them died during follow-up, against 26% and 28% for the 166 at 85 or below; this part's mean contribution to the log-risk is 0.25 for the faster group and -0.23 for the slower. The 161 patients with diastolic pressure at or below 76 mm Hg have a mean predicted risk of 48% against 27% for the 159 above. Switching the part off (its exit fixed at its mean over the training rows) lowers the AUC of the score against the event indicator from 0.833 to 0.822. Meaning: heart rate by itself predicts the part's exit with r² 0.62 (partial), and the clinical shock index, heart rate divided by systolic pressure, with r² 0.73 (partial) because the model weights diastolic rather than systolic pressure; the raw-unit difference heart rate minus diastolic pressure reaches r² 0.99, but that expression is close to the closed form itself, so beyond "fast heart rate with low diastolic pressure" the part is described, not explained. Proportional-hazards caveat: the model can represent a time-constant multiplicative effect of these measurements on the hazard and nothing else; this is not evidence that the effect is constant over follow-up.
ann_19.proposed: A higher heart rate raises the hazard steadily; higher diastolic and systolic blood pressure lower it steadily, the systolic by a small amount.

ann_20.original: This part is the weighted sum of three in-hospital-course inputs (congestive heart complications chf=1, cardiogenic shock sho=1 and length of stay los), read into the log-risk with weight one; the closed form is attached as evidence. In clinical units, congestive heart complications during the admission multiply the hazard by 2.08 (hazard ratio 1.40 per standard deviation of the indicator), cardiogenic shock multiplies it by 1.94 (1.13 per standard deviation) and each additional day in hospital by 1.010 (1.04 per standard deviation; 1.12-fold between the patients at the 5th and the 95th percentile of stay), each through its own edge. The model therefore gives a complicated in-hospital course a higher predicted risk, mostly through the heart-complication indicator. Self-probe (whole model; a constructed patient aged 72, body-mass index 27, heart rate 85, diastolic pressure 78 and systolic pressure 145 mm Hg, a 5-day stay, a non-Q-wave infarction): with heart complications and without shock the predicted 3-year risk of death is 52% (log-risk -0.18) against 29% (log-risk -0.91) with neither; adding cardiogenic shock to the heart-complication case raises it to 76% (log-risk 0.49); sweeping the stay of the typical case from 1 to 21 days moves the risk from 30% to 36%. On the training split 93 patients had heart complications, with a mean predicted 3-year risk of 64% and 73% of them died during follow-up, against 26% and 31% for the 227 without; this part's mean contribution to the log-risk is 0.56 with complications and -0.23 without. Cardiogenic shock is a small regime: the shock term is fitted to 11 training patients, of whom 64% died during follow-up (mean predicted risk 64%), and 100% of the 7 with both shock and heart complications died. Switching the part off (its exit fixed at its mean over the training rows) lowers the AUC of the score against the event indicator from 0.833 to 0.807. Meaning: the heart-complication indicator by itself predicts the part's exit with score 0.99 (meaningful); the shock and length-of-stay terms are small refinements on top of it. Proportional-hazards caveat: the model can represent a time-constant multiplicative effect of these events on the hazard and nothing else; this is not evidence that the effect is constant over follow-up.
ann_20.proposed: Congestive heart complications and cardiogenic shock raise the hazard; a longer stay raises it steadily by a small amount.

ann_21.original: A single term: the index infarction being Q-wave (mitype=1) rather than non-Q-wave, read into the log-risk with weight one; the closed form is attached as evidence. In clinical units a Q-wave infarction multiplies the hazard by 0.617 relative to a non-Q-wave infarction (hazard ratio 0.80 per standard deviation of the indicator), through its own edge: the model gives Q-wave infarctions a lower predicted risk. Self-probe (whole model; a constructed patient aged 72, body-mass index 27, heart rate 85, diastolic pressure 78 and systolic pressure 145 mm Hg, a 5-day stay, without heart complications or shock): a Q-wave infarction gives a predicted 3-year risk of death of 19% (log-risk -1.39) against 29% (log-risk -0.91) for a non-Q-wave infarction. On the training split the 92 Q-wave patients have a mean predicted 3-year risk of 22% and 26% of them died during follow-up, against 44% and 50% for the 228 non-Q-wave patients; this part's mean contribution to the log-risk is -0.34 for Q-wave and 0.14 for non-Q-wave patients (age and the Q-wave indicator are correlated at -0.28 in the training rows, so the other parts also differ between the two groups and the gap in mean risk is wider than this term alone makes it). Switching the part off (its exit fixed at its mean over the training rows) lowers the AUC of the score against the event indicator from 0.833 to 0.832, the smallest loss among the four parts. Meaning: the indicator itself predicts the part's exit with score 1.00, as it must for one input re-scaled; beyond the direction and size of its hazard ratio this leaf is described, not explained. Proportional-hazards caveat: the model can represent a time-constant multiplicative effect of infarction type on the hazard and nothing else; this is not evidence that the effect is constant over follow-up.
ann_21.proposed: A Q-wave index heart attack lowers the hazard.

ann_22.original: 0 = (identity_age_body + identity_haemo + identity_hospital + identity_mitype - 0.832): the output is the Cox log-risk g(x), the plain sum of the four parts plus a constant that the baseline hazard absorbs. The output activation is identity, so the hazard is the baseline hazard times exp(g(x)): the four parts are additive log-hazard-ratio terms and combine multiplicatively on the hazard, in parallel, with no gating or interaction between them (a sparse linear Cox model with nine input edges and no hidden node). The five inputs afb=1 (atrial fibrillation), av3=1 (complete heart block), cvd=1 (history of cardiovascular disease), gender=1 (female) and miord=1 (recurrent infarction) are not connected to the output in the phenotype (the coverage check's null basis) and are listed as entries of this root; the self-probe below shows that the prediction does not move when they change. sympy_srepr.y_0: Add(Mul(Float('0.371582', precision=13), Symbol('x_{age}')), Mul(Integer(-1), Float('0.241852', precision=13), Symbol('x_{bmi}')))

parts.name: age_and_body_mass
parts.original_hypothesis: identity_age_body = (0.372*age - 0.242*bmi) in standardised units, read into the log-risk with weight one: a plain weighted sum of two inputs. In clinical units, each additional year of age multiplies the hazard by 1.026 (hazard ratio 1.45 per standard deviation of age) and each additional kg/m² of body-mass index multiplies it by 0.957 (0.79 per standard deviation), each through its own edge. The model therefore gives older and thinner patients a higher predicted risk: between the patients at the 5th and the 95th percentile of age the age term changes the hazard 3.19-fold, and the body-mass term 2.29-fold. Self-probe (whole model, the other inputs held at the typical case): sweeping age from 45 to 95 years raises the predicted 3-year risk of death from 17% to 49%; sweeping body-mass index from 20 to 40 kg/m² lowers it from 38% to 18%. On the training split the 156 patients older than 72 have a mean predicted 3-year risk of 53% and 67% of them died during follow-up, against 22% and 20% for the 164 aged 72 or under; this part's mean contribution to the log-risk is 0.41 for the older group and -0.39 for the younger. Switching the part off (its exit fixed at its mean over the training rows) lowers the AUC of the score against the event indicator from 0.833 to 0.781, the largest loss among the four parts (the root lists them). Meaning: age by itself predicts the part's exit with r² 0.82 (meaningful); age and body-mass index are correlated at -0.40 in the training rows, so in the data the two terms partly offset each other. Proportional-hazards caveat: the model can represent a time-constant multiplicative effect of age and body-mass index on the hazard and nothing else; this is not evidence that the effect is constant over follow-up.

parts.name: in_hospital_course
parts.original_hypothesis: This part is the weighted sum of three in-hospital-course inputs (congestive heart complications chf=1, cardiogenic shock sho=1 and length of stay los), read into the log-risk with weight one; the closed form is attached as evidence. In clinical units, congestive heart complications during the admission multiply the hazard by 2.08 (hazard ratio 1.40 per standard deviation of the indicator), cardiogenic shock multiplies it by 1.94 (1.13 per standard deviation) and each additional day in hospital by 1.010 (1.04 per standard deviation; 1.12-fold between the patients at the 5th and the 95th percentile of stay), each through its own edge. The model therefore gives a complicated in-hospital course a higher predicted risk, mostly through the heart-complication indicator. Self-probe (whole model; a constructed patient aged 72, body-mass index 27, heart rate 85, diastolic pressure 78 and systolic pressure 145 mm Hg, a 5-day stay, a non-Q-wave infarction): with heart complications and without shock the predicted 3-year risk of death is 52% (log-risk -0.18) against 29% (log-risk -0.91) with neither; adding cardiogenic shock to the heart-complication case raises it to 76% (log-risk 0.49); sweeping the stay of the typical case from 1 to 21 days moves the risk from 30% to 36%. On the training split 93 patients had heart complications, with a mean predicted 3-year risk of 64% and 73% of them died during follow-up, against 26% and 31% for the 227 without; this part's mean contribution to the log-risk is 0.56 with complications and -0.23 without. Cardiogenic shock is a small regime: the shock term is fitted to 11 training patients, of whom 64% died during follow-up (mean predicted risk 64%), and 100% of the 7 with both shock and heart complications died. Switching the part off (its exit fixed at its mean over the training rows) lowers the AUC of the score against the event indicator from 0.833 to 0.807. Meaning: the heart-complication indicator by itself predicts the part's exit with score 0.99 (meaningful); the shock and length-of-stay terms are small refinements on top of it. Proportional-hazards caveat: the model can represent a time-constant multiplicative effect of these events on the hazard and nothing else; this is not evidence that the effect is constant over follow-up.

parts.name: admission_haemodynamics
parts.original_hypothesis: identity_haemo = (0.286*hr - 0.199*diasbp - 0.0289*sysbp) in standardised units, read into the log-risk with weight one: a plain weighted sum of the three admission haemodynamic measurements. In clinical units, each additional beat per minute of admission heart rate multiplies the hazard by 1.0121 (1.33 per standard deviation), each additional mm Hg of diastolic blood pressure multiplies it by 0.9908 (0.82 per standard deviation), and each additional mm Hg of systolic blood pressure by 0.9991 (0.972 per standard deviation), each through its own edge. The systolic term is small: between the patients at the 5th and the 95th percentile it changes the hazard 1.10-fold, against 2.44-fold for heart rate and 1.82-fold for diastolic pressure. The model therefore gives a faster heart rate and a lower diastolic pressure at admission a higher predicted risk, a reading of haemodynamic strain. Self-probe (whole model, the other inputs held at the typical case): sweeping heart rate from 50 to 150 beats per minute raises the predicted 3-year risk of death from 22% to 56%; sweeping diastolic pressure from 50 to 120 mm Hg lowers it from 38% to 22%; sweeping systolic pressure from 90 to 200 mm Hg moves it from 32% to 30%. On the training split the 154 patients with an admission heart rate above 85 have a mean predicted 3-year risk of 49% and 59% of them died during follow-up, against 26% and 28% for the 166 at 85 or below; this part's mean contribution to the log-risk is 0.25 for the faster group and -0.23 for the slower. The 161 patients with diastolic pressure at or below 76 mm Hg have a mean predicted risk of 48% against 27% for the 159 above. Switching the part off (its exit fixed at its mean over the training rows) lowers the AUC of the score against the event indicator from 0.833 to 0.822. Meaning: heart rate by itself predicts the part's exit with r² 0.62 (partial), and the clinical shock index, heart rate divided by systolic pressure, with r² 0.73 (partial) because the model weights diastolic rather than systolic pressure; the raw-unit difference heart rate minus diastolic pressure reaches r² 0.99, but that expression is close to the closed form itself, so beyond "fast heart rate with low diastolic pressure" the part is described, not explained. Proportional-hazards caveat: the model can represent a time-constant multiplicative effect of these measurements on the hazard and nothing else; this is not evidence that the effect is constant over follow-up.

closed_form.rounding: weights and biases at 3 significant figures

parts.name: index_mi_type
parts.original_hypothesis: A single term: the index infarction being Q-wave (mitype=1) rather than non-Q-wave, read into the log-risk with weight one; the closed form is attached as evidence. In clinical units a Q-wave infarction multiplies the hazard by 0.617 relative to a non-Q-wave infarction (hazard ratio 0.80 per standard deviation of the indicator), through its own edge: the model gives Q-wave infarctions a lower predicted risk. Self-probe (whole model; a constructed patient aged 72, body-mass index 27, heart rate 85, diastolic pressure 78 and systolic pressure 145 mm Hg, a 5-day stay, without heart complications or shock): a Q-wave infarction gives a predicted 3-year risk of death of 19% (log-risk -1.39) against 29% (log-risk -0.91) for a non-Q-wave infarction. On the training split the 92 Q-wave patients have a mean predicted 3-year risk of 22% and 26% of them died during follow-up, against 44% and 50% for the 228 non-Q-wave patients; this part's mean contribution to the log-risk is -0.34 for Q-wave and 0.14 for non-Q-wave patients (age and the Q-wave indicator are correlated at -0.28 in the training rows, so the other parts also differ between the two groups and the gap in mean risk is wider than this term alone makes it). Switching the part off (its exit fixed at its mean over the training rows) lowers the AUC of the score against the event indicator from 0.833 to 0.832, the smallest loss among the four parts. Meaning: the indicator itself predicts the part's exit with score 1.00, as it must for one input re-scaled; beyond the direction and size of its hazard ratio this leaf is described, not explained. Proportional-hazards caveat: the model can represent a time-constant multiplicative effect of infarction type on the hazard and nothing else; this is not evidence that the effect is constant over follow-up.

confidence_rules.clearly: a meaningful change in predicted risk for a typical patient (at least 5% points), the test split agrees (same sign, and its bootstrap interval over test patients excludes no benefit), and every group has at least 20 training patients
confidence_rules.consistently across patients: the claim holds for at least 90% of training patients (range across patients); this is not a significance statement
confidence_rules.on the training data only: the test split disagrees (opposite sign, or no benefit on test patients) or is unclear (its interval includes no benefit), or no test check is available
confidence_rules.slightly: the change in predicted risk for a typical patient is below 5% points
confidence_rules.the model has little data on this: a compared group has fewer than 20 training patients

summary.text: The model treats a higher age at admission as clearly raising the predicted 3-year risk of death steadily: for a typical patient, it goes from about 19% at 50 years to about 42% at 87 years, a hazard ratio of about 2.6.

For a typical patient, the model gives a higher predicted 3-year risk of death if the patient has congestive heart complications (about 54%) than if the patient has no congestive heart complications (about 31%), a hazard ratio of about 2.1 (on the training data only).

The model treats a higher heart rate at admission as raising the predicted 3-year risk of death steadily: for a typical patient, it goes from about 24% at 58 beats per minute to about 42% at 117 beats per minute, a hazard ratio of about 2 (on the training data only).
The model ignores atrial fibrillation, complete heart block, history of cardiovascular disease, female sex and recurrent heart attack.

Each effect multiplies the hazard by the same amount at every point of follow-up, because the model has no way to represent an effect that changes with time (the proportional-hazards assumption); this is not evidence that the effect is constant over time.
